content.heading: A Minor Piano Chord (Am)
paragraphs: The A minor chord, written Am, contains A, C, and E. All three are white-key notes. In root position, play A as the lowest note, with C and E above it.
The example below uses A3–C4–E4, with C4 as middle C. Listen to these notes together or individually, then compare the two inversions.

content.heading: Find A, C, and E on the keyboard
paragraphs: Start with C4, middle C. A3 is two white-key steps to its left: move past B3 to A3. E4 is two white-key steps to the right of C4: move past D4 to E4.
The marked keys show pitches, not a hand shape or a required fingering.
steps: Locate A3, C4, and E4 using the labels.
Play them separately to check their order, then sound the three notes together.
If you use another octave, move all three notes by the same number of octaves to keep this root-position shape.

content.heading: A minor inversions
paragraphs: An inversion changes which chord tone is lowest. First inversion puts C in the bass; second inversion puts E in the bass. The letters after the slash in Am/C and Am/E identify that bass note.
These examples use close position without doubled notes. Other spacings are possible; the lowest note determines the inversion.

content.heading: What makes this chord minor?
paragraphs: From A to C is a minor third: three semitone steps. From C to E is a major third: four semitone steps. Together, the outer notes A and E form a perfect fifth.
Compare A minor, A–C–E, with A major, A–C♯–E. Only the third changes. A minor uses C natural; A major uses C-sharp. The interval pattern identifies the chord as minor, without needing a mood label.

paragraphs: Use this as a note-finding check. Work with one position at a time before moving to the next.
steps: Play A3–C4–E4 and say “A in the bass.”
Choose first inversion and play C4–E4–A4. Say “C in the bass.”
Choose second inversion and play E4–A4–C5. Say “E in the bass.”
Without looking at the chord symbol, name the lowest note and identify the position. Check against the table.

rows: Is Am the same as A minor?
Yes. Am is a common chord symbol for the A minor triad. You may also see A min or A−.
Does Am/C become a C chord?
No. It is still A minor, with C as the lowest note. Its chord tones are still A, C, and E.
Is Am the same as Am7?
No. Am is A–C–E; Am7 adds G. This page covers the three-note Am chord.
Are the numbers in A3, C4, and E4 finger numbers?
No. They identify octaves. The diagrams in this reference do not prescribe fingering.
